title: CSAT comprehension: three passages
note: Three original passages written for this app, each with five questions in the CSAT style. English only.
sources: Original passages written by our editors; question styles follow recent UPSC CSAT papers (upsc.gov.in)
verify: Read each passage and its five questions together: check that every answer follows from the passage alone, and that no wrong option is also defensible.

sets.title: The water beneath the city
sets.passage:
Most Indian cities were built near water, and for centuries they managed it with modest means. Tanks, step-wells and lakes caught the monsoon and released it slowly through the dry months. Many of these were not owned by any single person. A village or a neighbourhood looked after them because everyone drew from them, and everyone knew who did not do their share.

As cities grew, piped supply arrived, and the old system seemed unnecessary. Tanks were filled in to make bus stands and housing colonies. Storm drains were lined with concrete so that rain would leave the city as fast as possible. The logic was simple: water was something to be brought in from a distant reservoir, and rain was a nuisance to be carried away.

The trouble is that the piped supply rarely kept up. Households and businesses that could afford it dug borewells, and then dug them deeper as the water table fell. Groundwater, unlike a lake, is invisible. No one sees it shrinking, and no single well appears to be the cause. Each owner, acting sensibly for himself, adds to a loss that harms all. When the shortage finally becomes visible, it is usually as a crisis: tankers in the streets, and wells that suddenly run dry.

Floods and droughts in the same city are often treated as two separate problems, handled by two separate departments. They are better understood as one. A city that hurries its rain into drains in July is the same city that buys water from tankers in April. The paved surfaces that make floods worse are the same surfaces that stop rain from soaking into the ground.

None of this means that cities should return to the past. Old tanks cannot supply millions of people, and the communities that once kept them have changed. But the principle behind them still holds. Water that is stored close to where it falls is cheaper, and a resource that people can see is a resource they are more likely to protect. The more useful question is not whether to rely on reservoirs or on local storage, but how to make each support the other.

questions.q: Which one of the following best reflects the central idea of the passage?
options: Cities should give up piped water supply and return to traditional tanks.
Communities no longer care about shared resources.
Urban floods and water shortages are linked, and local storage should work together with distant supply.
Borewells are the main cause of urban floods.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph joins floods and shortages into one problem, and the last says reservoirs and local storage should support each other. The first option is ruled out by 'None of this means that cities should return to the past'.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does the fall in groundwater tend to go unnoticed until there is a crisis?
options: Groundwater cannot be seen, and no single well appears to be the cause.
Governments do not publish data on water tables.
Borewells are dug only by businesses, not by households.
The piped supply always makes up for the loss.
questions.why: The third paragraph says groundwater 'is invisible. No one sees it shrinking, and no single well appears to be the cause.' Nothing is said about data, and the passage says households too dig borewells.

questions.q: Which one of the following is an assumption implicit in the statement that 'a resource that people can see is a resource they are more likely to protect'?
options: People protect only what they own personally.
Resources that cannot be seen have no economic value.
Local communities manage every resource better than governments do.
Seeing the condition of a resource encourages people to act to conserve it.
questions.why: The claim links visibility to protective action, so it assumes that seeing a resource's state prompts people to look after it. The passage itself describes shared tanks that no one owned, which rules out the first option; the other two go far beyond the text.

statements: The author holds that traditional tanks can meet the needs of today's large cities.
The author suggests that paved surfaces worsen both flooding and the shortage of groundwater.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are valid according to the passage?
options: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
questions.why: Statement 1 is contradicted: 'Old tanks cannot supply millions of people.' Statement 2 is stated in the fourth paragraph: the surfaces that make floods worse also stop rain from soaking into the ground.

questions.q: The behaviour of borewell owners described in the third paragraph is best described as
options: a case where choices that are sensible for each person together cause a shared loss
a failure of government alone
deliberate waste of water by the rich
a market in which the price of water is set correctly
questions.why: 'Each owner, acting sensibly for himself, adds to a loss that harms all' is the classic problem of a shared resource. The passage does not call the owners wasteful, and it does not blame government alone.

sets.title: Feeling ready and being ready
sets.passage:
There is a kind of confidence that comes from never having been tested. A student who has read a chapter five times may feel that she knows it, and the feeling is genuine. But familiarity is not the same as understanding. Recognising a page when you see it again is easier than producing its ideas from memory, and much easier than using them on a problem you have not met before.

Research on learning has repeatedly found that people judge their own knowledge poorly. They tend to prefer the methods that feel smooth, such as rereading and highlighting, over the methods that feel difficult, such as testing themselves or explaining an idea to someone else. Yet the difficult methods usually produce more durable learning. The struggle to recall something is not a sign that learning is failing; often it is the learning.

This creates an awkward situation. The study methods that feel best in the moment are often the ones that help least, and the methods that help most make us feel, while we use them, that we are doing badly. A learner who trusts only her feelings may therefore drift toward comfort and away from progress.

Mistakes play a particular role here. An error made during practice, and then corrected, tends to be remembered better than a fact that was simply read. The surprise of being wrong seems to mark the correction as important. This is one reason why a practice test is more than a measure of what one knows; it is itself a way of learning.

It does not follow that every difficulty is useful. Material that is far beyond a learner's current level produces confusion rather than learning, and constant failure can drain motivation. The aim is a level of challenge that stretches without overwhelming. Nor does it follow that feelings are worthless. They are simply an unreliable guide to one question in particular: how well do I really know this?

The practical lesson is modest. Before deciding that a topic is finished, a learner can close the book and try to write down what she knows. The gap between what she expected to recall and what she actually recalls is useful information. It is better to discover that gap at a desk than in an examination hall.

questions.q: Which one of the following is the most logical and rational inference that can be made from the passage?
options: Rereading is useless and should never be done.
Students who make mistakes in practice will fail their examinations.
Learners should always choose the most difficult material available.
How easy a study method feels is not a reliable sign of how much it helps.
questions.why: The third paragraph says the methods that feel best often help least, and the ones that help most feel bad. The first option overstates the case, the second reverses the passage's view of mistakes, and the third is contradicted by the fifth paragraph.

questions.q: According to the passage, why is an error made and corrected during practice remembered well?
options: Because the surprise of being wrong seems to mark the correction as important.
Because errors in practice are rare.
Because a correction is always followed by rereading.
Because teachers give extra marks for corrections.
questions.why: The fourth paragraph says: 'The surprise of being wrong seems to mark the correction as important.' The other options are not in the passage.

questions.q: With reference to the passage, the following assumptions have been made:
statements: Learners can improve their learning, at least in part, by changing how they study.
Feelings are of no use in any aspect of learning.
questions.ask: Which of the above assumptions is/are valid?
options: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
questions.why: The whole passage recommends better methods, such as self-testing, which assumes that changing methods helps. Assumption 2 is contradicted: 'Nor does it follow that feelings are worthless.'

questions.q: Which one of the following best describes the author's view of difficulty in learning?
options: Difficulty should be avoided because it lowers motivation.
Difficulty helps when it stretches the learner without overwhelming them.
All difficulty is useful, however great.
Difficulty matters only during examinations.
questions.why: The fifth paragraph says 'The aim is a level of challenge that stretches without overwhelming.' The author rejects both extremes: difficulty can help, but material far beyond one's level causes confusion.

questions.q: The statement 'familiarity is not the same as understanding' implies that
options: students should never read a chapter more than once
understanding can come only from a teacher
recognising material is a weaker test of knowledge than recalling it and using it
familiar material is always forgotten
questions.why: The next sentence explains it: recognising a page is easier than producing its ideas from memory, and much easier than using them on a new problem. The passage does not forbid rereading or mention teachers.

sets.title: When a pilot grows up
sets.passage:
When a new policy works well in a small trial, the natural next step is to expand it. Yet many programmes that succeed in a few districts disappoint when they are rolled out across a country. The reasons are worth understanding, because they say something about how evidence travels.

The first reason is the people involved. A pilot is often run by a motivated team that chose the work and is closely watched. When the programme expands, it is run by ordinary officials who have many other duties and no special interest in this one. The idea is the same; the effort behind it is not.

The second reason is the setting. A trial may be placed in districts that are easier to work in, with better roads, more literate populations or more cooperative local leaders. Results from such places may not hold in harder ones. What worked, worked somewhere in particular.

The third reason is subtler. A small programme does not change the world around it, but a large one can. If a few hundred farmers in a trial are given a better seed, the price of their crop is unaffected. If millions are given it, the harvest may rise enough to lower the price, and the gain to each farmer may shrink. Effects that are invisible at small scale can dominate at large scale.

None of this means trials are pointless. They remain far better than guesses or slogans. A policy that fails in a careful trial is unlikely to succeed at scale, so trials are good at ruling ideas out. They are less good at guaranteeing that an idea will work everywhere.

The sensible response is to treat expansion itself as a series of experiments. A programme can be extended in stages, with honest measurement at each stage, and with the expectation that it will need adjusting. Those who design policy should ask not only whether it worked, but also why it worked, for whom, and whether those reasons would still be present elsewhere. The answers are rarely as tidy as the original trial, but they are much closer to the truth.

questions.q: Which one of the following best expresses the central theme of the passage?
options: Small trials are a waste of public money.
Officials are less honest than the teams that run pilots.
Agricultural policies always fail when they are expanded.
Success in a small trial does not guarantee success at scale, so expansion should be gradual and measured.
questions.why: The passage gives three reasons why scaled-up programmes disappoint and ends by recommending staged expansion with measurement. It defends trials, so the first option is wrong; it never questions officials' honesty, only their motivation.

questions.q: The example of the better seed in the fourth paragraph is used to show that
options: farmers are unwilling to adopt new seeds
a large programme can change market conditions in a way that a small one cannot
trials should be held only in poor districts
crop prices do not change with the size of the harvest
questions.why: The point is that a few hundred farmers do not move the price, but millions can, shrinking each farmer's gain: 'Effects that are invisible at small scale can dominate at large scale.' The last option is the opposite of the example.

statements: According to the passage, trials are more useful for rejecting weak ideas than for proving that an idea will work everywhere.
The author believes that pilots should be stopped and policies designed from theory alone.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
options: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
questions.why: Statement 1 restates the fifth paragraph: trials 'are good at ruling ideas out' and 'less good at guaranteeing that an idea will work everywhere'. Statement 2 is contradicted: trials 'remain far better than guesses or slogans'.

questions.q: The author's advice to extend programmes in stages rests mainly on which one of the following assumptions?
options: The conditions that made a trial succeed may not be present in every new area.
Officials will refuse to carry out any new programme.
Every programme will fail sooner or later.
Measurement is impossible once a programme is large.
questions.why: Staged expansion with measurement makes sense only if results may change from place to place, which is the point of the 'why, for whom, and elsewhere' questions. The passage asks for measurement at each stage, so it assumes measurement is possible.

questions.q: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the second reason the author gives for why programmes disappoint at scale?
options: The team that ran the trial was highly motivated.
The price of the crop fell after the programme expanded.
The trial districts were chosen at random from all the districts of the state.
The officials who ran the expanded programme had many other duties.
questions.why: The second reason is that trials are placed in easier districts. If the trial districts were picked at random, they would not be systematically easier, which weakens that reason. The other options support the first or third reasons, or are irrelevant to the second.
